passage: Dear Bua, Last Sunday Papa was doing the accounts and said, "Vijay's coaching fees come first. Rekha, start saving for your shaadi." He said it lightly, and Dadi nodded: "A daughter's share is her wedding." I smiled and washed the dishes, but all night I felt like a bill someone had to pay. I am fifteen and I came first in maths, Bua. Then yesterday Mummy mentioned your call, and Papa put his tea down. He said, "Both of you will study as far as you wish. Wedding savings can wait." I didn't know what to say. My brother Vijay looked up and said, "Then we both get the tutor." I am still learning to believe it. Please come for Diwali. Rekha

passage: Kirti, listen, I have to tell someone. At Shweta didi's wedding yesterday, Fufa was eating jalebi and told Mummy loudly, "Put money aside for Lalita's shaadi. Spend on the boy's coaching. Vijay's the one who'll earn." Mummy was holding a plate. I stood right beside her. I'm fourteen, the girl in the family whose marks were higher than my brother's last term, but suddenly I felt like a cost that needed managing. My ears went hot. I wanted to vanish behind the stage flowers. Then Mummy said, quite calmly, "Both my children will study as far as they want, Bhaiya. Lalita's fees are fees, not a wedding fund." Fufa shrugged and reached for another jalebi. Vijay whispered, "I'll buy you a pen for your exam." It was such a small thing. But I'm still smiling.

passage:
Trisha had forty minutes before the coaching centre closed its admission counter, and her mother was still counting notes at the kitchen table.
"There isn't enough for both," Ma said. "Jatin's engineering coaching comes first. And we have to keep adding to your wedding fund, Trisha. That's your future."
Trisha, fifteen, looked at the form in her hand, the science batch she had topped the test for. "My future is the wedding?"
Jatin, seventeen, looked up from his phone. "Ma, she scored higher than me in the entrance test."
Ma's hands paused. "People will say we spent on the girl and not the boy."
"Let them," Jatin said. "I'll take the cheaper weekend batch."
Ma stared at them both. Then she pushed some of the notes toward Trisha. "Go. Run, before they close."
Trisha ran, her eyes stinging.

qa.q: How long did Trisha have before the admission counter closed?
qa.a: Trisha had forty minutes before the coaching centre closed its admission counter.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she asked, "My future is the wedding?"
qa.a: She felt hurt and small, as if her own schooling mattered less than a wedding fund and her brother's coaching.

qa.q: Which choice made things fairer, and why?
qa.a: Jatin offered to take the cheaper weekend batch because Trisha had scored higher; sharing the cost fairly gave both of them a chance at school.

qa.q: Why might Ma react differently at the end?
qa.a: Hearing Jatin speak up and seeing Trisha's result, Ma may have felt the unfairness more clearly than her fear of what people would say.

grounding: Under money and time pressure, a teenage girl hears that her future is her wedding fund and her brother's schooling comes first, before fair encouragement wins.

In the staffroom of the girls' school in Tiruchi, Aditi Miss found Kavitha, sixteen, crying over a scholarship form.
"My Appa says there's no point. My brother gets college. For me, they're buying gold every year for my marriage." Kavitha wiped her face. "He says I'm a responsibility."
Aditi Miss sat beside her. "What do you want to study?"
"Chemistry. But maybe I'm being selfish."
"Wanting to learn isn't selfish. You're in the top five of the class." Aditi Miss pulled up the scholarship details. "This covers the whole fee. Shall I talk to your Appa with you?"
On Saturday, Kavitha's father came to school, arms crossed. Aditi Miss showed him Kavitha's marks, one by one. He was silent for a long time. Then he said, "Top five?" and signed the form.

qa.q: What subject does Kavitha want to study?
qa.a: Kavitha wants to study chemistry.

qa.q: Why does Kavitha think she might be selfish?
qa.a: Her father calls her a responsibility and puts her brother's college first, so she feels guilty and like a burden for wanting education.

qa.q: How did Aditi Miss support Kavitha well?
qa.a: She told Kavitha that wanting to learn isn't selfish, found a scholarship that covers the fee, and met the father together with Kavitha, showing him her marks.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's father have seen his daughter differently after seeing her marks?
qa.a: He may have started to see her as a capable student worth investing in, rather than only as someone to marry off.

grounding: It shows a teenage girl told that her brother's schooling comes first and that gold is saved for her marriage, and a teacher's fair encouragement.

"Parul, don't fill that form for the science camp. Save the fee. Every rupee counts for your wedding," Bua called from the sofa.
Parul froze with the pen in her hand. Irfan, her classmate from next door, was sitting beside her with his own form.
"But Bua, Bhaiya went to the camp last year."
"He's a boy. He'll earn for the family."
Parul's voice went very small. "So I'm only a cost?"
From the kitchen, Ma came out, drying her hands. "Parul, who told you that?" She looked at Bua. "Didi, she's fifteen. Her schooling is her future, same as her brother's."
Bua huffed. "In our time—"
"In our time, I wasn't allowed to finish Class ten," Ma said quietly. "Fill it in, Parul."
Irfan pushed the pen back toward Parul and grinned. "Tick the robotics option. You're better at it than me."

qa.q: Which option does Irfan tell Parul to tick?
qa.a: Irfan tells Parul to tick the robotics option.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when she asked if she was only a cost?
qa.a: She felt hurt and like a burden, because Bua said her fee should be saved for her wedding while her brother had gone to the camp.

qa.q: What made Ma's response fair?
qa.a: Ma said Parul's schooling was her future, the same as her brother's, and shared her own story of not finishing Class ten, which gave Parul equal support.

qa.q: How might Irfan see what happened?
qa.a: Irfan, as a classmate, sees Parul as a capable student, so he probably felt uncomfortable at Bua's words and glad to encourage her.

grounding: It shows a teenage girl told that her fee should be saved for her wedding while her brother studies, and her mother's fair insistence on equal schooling.

passage:
It was two years ago, when I was fourteen, but I still remember that evening. I heard Amma and Appa in the kitchen. "Keerthana's gold is coming along. The chit fund will cover her wedding." Then: "Coaching for Karthik's engineering is expensive, but he's a boy, his future matters." I stood in the corridor holding my maths book. I had topped the district in maths. Karthik hadn't. I felt like a bill the family was paying off slowly.
For weeks I stopped raising my hand in class. Neelam ma'am, my maths teacher, noticed. She asked me to stay after school, and I told her everything, crying. She didn't criticise my parents. She said, "Your mind is not a burden. It is a gift." Then she came home with me and spoke to Appa about the scholarship exam. Appa was quiet for a long time. That summer, both Karthik and I started coaching.

qa.q: What had Keerthana topped the district in?
qa.a: In maths.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel after overhearing her parents in the kitchen?
qa.a: She felt hurt and worthless, like a bill the family was paying off, and stopped raising her hand in class.

qa.q: What did Neelam ma'am do that was fair?
qa.a: She encouraged Keerthana's ability, told her she was not a burden, and spoke to Appa about equal chances, which led to both children getting coaching.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when Neelam ma'am spoke to him?
qa.a: Appa was probably surprised and thoughtful, perhaps realising for the first time how unequal the plans had been.

grounding: It illustrates a teenage girl who hears the family saves for her wedding while her brother's education comes first, and how equal schooling is the fair answer.
